CausalChain: Oxidative stress in the HCC microenvironment -> Activation of m6A writer enzymes -> m6A modification of hypoxia-responsive lncRNAs -> Enhanced binding of modified lncRNAs with HIF-1α-stabilizing RNA-binding proteins -> Increased stabilization of HIF-1α mRNA -> Elevated HIF-1α protein levels -> Promotion of angiogenesis and HCC progression
Hypothesis: Oxidative stress in HCC leads to increased m6A modification of hypoxia-responsive lncRNAs, which enhances their interaction with RNA-binding proteins that stabilize HIF-1α mRNA. This process drives higher HIF-1α levels, promoting angiogenesis and facilitating a feedforward loop in HCC tumor progression.
Abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the multifaceted roles of long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) in the regulation of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression. Building upon data that lncRNAs mediate responses to hypoxia, oxidative stress and epigenetic modification, we propose that oxidative stress encountered in HCC microenvironments induces m6A modification of hypoxia-responsive lncRNAs. These chemical modifications, in turn, enhance the binding of these lncRNAs to specific RNA-binding proteins that stabilize HIF-1α mRNA. This stabilization promotes angiogenesis and further tumor progression, creating a feedforward loop that exacerbates HCC aggressiveness. Our hypothesis provides a novel mechanistic link between oxidative stress, RNA modification, and the regulation of hypoxia signaling, thereby suggesting new avenues for therapeutic intervention in HCC.
